name: Dusky Dull Green
lede: Dusky Dull Green is a very dark, grayed green first plated by Robert Ridgway in 1912, favored by Gauguin and Cezanne far more than our archive's average.

sections.title: A 1912 plate
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* of 1912 plates this swatch at plate XLII, hue 37 triple-prime, on an aged, scanned original that is itself approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS charts of 1955 file block 151 as a dark grayish green, 5.9 units from this swatch [1]. The name pairs *dusky dull* with [[green]] [1].

At hex #2F504B it measures lightness 13 and chroma 14 in LCH, among the darkest named greens in the library [1]. Its closest named neighbors are [[samara|Samara]], 2.7 units away and bluer, and [[dark-slate-grey|Dark Slate Grey]], 2.8 units off, also bluer; [[dusky-bluish-green|Dusky Bluish Green]] sits 4.0 units off and lighter [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 1.04% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (247 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 118 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 61% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.5% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (25 paintings), 2.8 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 40% of its 118 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Paul Cezanne, present in 9 of 50 works here, 10.1x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 8.0x) [3]. It is most over-represented in France, 2.1x expected (42 of 3,443 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1000, 912 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
